events.text: The Peak District becomes Britain's first national park
UNESCO adopts the World Heritage Convention
Yellowstone becomes the first national park in the United States
The Grand Canyon is made a national park by act of Congress

reveal.explanation: Yellowstone was set apart in 1872, forty-seven years before Congress made a national park of the Grand Canyon in 1919. Britain came to the idea later, designating the Peak District in 1951, and UNESCO adopted the convention that created World Heritage Sites in 1972.

sources.excerpt: It was established by the 42nd U.S. Congress through the Yellowstone National Park Protection Act and signed into law by President Ulysses S. Grant on March 1, 1872.

Further Senate bills to establish the site as a national park were introduced and defeated in 1910 and 1911, before the Grand Canyon National Park Act (Pub. L. 65–277) was finally signed by President Woodrow Wilson on February 26, 1919.
The Peak District National Park became the United Kingdom's first national park on 17 April 1951.

Based on the draft convention that UNESCO had initiated, a single text was eventually agreed upon by all parties, and the "Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage" was adopted by the General Conference of UNESCO on 16 November 1972.

editorNotes: Yellowstone: the page states 1872 without qualification but is firmer about the United States than about the world, saying Yellowstone was the first national park in the US and is also widely understood to be the first national park in the world, so the event text claims only the American first; the same page gives the signing as 1 March 1872 in both the lede and the history section. Grand Canyon: the canyon was a forest reserve from 1893 and a national monument from 11 January 1908, and earlier park bills failed in 1910 and 1911, so the text specifies the act of Congress of 26 February 1919; its later listing as a World Heritage Site in 1979 was avoided to keep it clear of the fourth entry. Peak District: designated on 17 April 1951 under the National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act of 1949, with the Lake District and Snowdonia following later the same year, so the text says first rather than naming a month. World Heritage Convention: the page gives 16 November 1972 for adoption by the General Conference and 23 November 1972 for signature, both in the same year, with entry into force in 1975; the first inscriptions of 1978 were considered as an alternative event and rejected as less clearly a founding moment.
